statement.paragraphs: Let $\phi : R \longrightarrow R'$ be a ring homomorphism. Then, the image of $\phi$: \[ \im \phi = \{r' \in R' : r' = \phi(r) \text{ for some } r \in R\} \] is a ring under the addition and multiplication operations of $R'$. (In fact, it is a subring of $R'$.)

Let $m$ be a natural number. Consider the map $\phi : \mathbb{Z} \ra \ZZ_m$ defined by: \[ \phi(n) = {n}_m, \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{Z}, \] where ${n}_m$ is the remainder of the division of $n$ by $m$.
It is clear that $\phi$ is surjective, and that $\ker \phi = m\ZZ$. So, it follows from the First Isomorphism Theorem that: \[ \ZZ_m \cong \ZZ/m\ZZ. \]

statement.title: Correspondence Theorem for Rings
Correspondence Theorem for Rings
statement.paragraphs: Let $R$ be commutative ring, and $I$ a proper ideal of $R$. Then, the natural map $\pi : R \longrightarrow R/I$ induces a bijection $\pi'$ of between the set of ideals of $R/I$ and the set of all ideals of $R$ which contains $I$.

More precisely, for each ideal $J$ of $R$ which contains $I$: \[ \pi' : J \mapsto J/I := \{a + I : a \in J\} \] This bijection is ``inclusion-perserving", in the sense that if we have the following chain of inclusion of ideals $I \subseteq J' \subseteq J$ in $R$, then: \[ \pi'(J') \subseteq \pi'(J). \]
